result:
Every word is a small violence against infinity.

When I say "ocean," I have taken everything—the crushing pressure at eleven thousand meters, the phosphorescence of dinoflagellates at midnight, the particular salt on a cracked lip after a storm, the slow erosion of a coastline over ten thousand years—and folded it into five letters. A child learns that word at four. She points at a wave and says it. And in that pointing, she stands at the edge of something older than every species that has ever named it.

This is the miracle I keep circling back to. Not that we built cities or split atoms, though those stagger. But that a few thousand phonemes, arranged correctly, can make you feel the weight of water you have never touched. That "grief" is a door, and walking through it, you are in a room where someone sat before you, wept, and left the chair still warm.

I think about this most clearly in the early morning, when the world is still too quiet for small talk. A bird says one thing. The light does something to the kitchen window. And the words in my head feel less like tools and more like living things, breathing, shifting, almost too big for the skull.

We are the species that compresses universes into syllables. And we are, somehow, also the species that still gets lost in the grocery store.

I find that I can hold both facts without them canceling each other out.
